newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia claims success against "massive" spy wave. [CORRECTED 13:57 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Russia claims success against "massive" spy wave. [CORRECTED 13:57 GMT]

text.p: Foreign spies are burrowing across Russia more actively than at any time since World War Two but Moscow's chief spycatcher said on Friday his new double agent hotline had stopped many of the moles in their tracks.

"Not at any time in the recent history of our country have we exposed such spy networks. We are uncovering a simply massive number," said Nikolai (corrects first name from Valentin) Kovalyov, head of the Federal Security Service (FSB), successor to the Soviet KGB.
In an interview with Moskovsky Komsomolets daily, he said he was shocked by how cheaply many Russians were prepared to sell out their country.
But he claimed great success for the hotline, set up a month ago to invite Russians spying for foreign powers to turn themselves in to the FSB and become double agents.

"We've had several hundred interesting calls," he said. "Real information turned up on various secret services. Several foreign intelligence services have already reacted to this by completely winding up agent operations on Russian territory."
His comments came after a week in which the authorities have given great play to the sentencing of two Russians, convicted separately of spying for Britain and the United States.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday sentenced a former defence company manager to 10 years' hard labour and confiscated his property for spying for London's MI6. Vadim Sintsov, 62, said he earned $12,000 in a year by selling data on the arms trade.

On Thursday, the eve of the U.S. Independence Day holiday, it was reported that a Moscow court had last month sentenced a former Soviet diplomat to seven years of hard labour for taking $20,000 for spying on behalf of the CIA for years.

"As a rule, the basis for treason is a purely mercantile motivation. We don't know of a single case lately where someone has become a traitor out of not agreeing with current politics. It's all down to money," Kovalyov said.

"It's surprising to see for what miserable sums people will destroy their destinies," he said, noting a recent case in which a suspect was ready to sell secret information for just $3,000 -- still more than a year's pay for the average Russia.
"If that material would have got into the hands of foreign secret services, the damage to Russia would have cost no less than $300 million," he said.

Russian officials say the interest in Russia from supposedly now friendly powers has increased, not declined, after the Cold War because of a hunger for commercial information, especially dealing with Russia's successful arms industry and other sectors.

Foreign diplomats -- some of whom have been expelled in recent years for links to spy networks -- say Western governments are also keen for data on organised crime in Russia and its suspected links to state officials.
FSB officials have said they caught 27 professional foreign spies last year and 60 Russians in the pay of foreign powers.
Among those still waiting trial is a Russian foreign ministry employee, Platon Obukhov, arrested last year and accused of spying for London.
Shrugging off ironic comment in the media about his "spy hotline", Kovalyov repeated: "I want to use this occasion to remind people that the number is 224-3500."
